html:
The battle near Pydna in northern Greece in 168 BCE where a Roman army under the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus destroyed the army of Perseus, the last king of Macedon. It ended the Third Macedonian War.

The Macedonian phalanx, a dense block of men with very long pikes, was hard to beat head on. On broken ground its lines opened up, and the smaller Roman units of the legion pushed into the gaps and cut it apart. Ancient writers saw the battle as the moment the legion proved itself against the army that Alexander had led.

Perseus fled, was caught, and was paraded in Paullus's triumph in Rome. The Antigonid kingdom was abolished and Macedon was split into four republics that paid tribute to Rome. After a revolt they were made a single Roman province in 146 BCE.

Rome also punished Greeks it thought had wavered. Rhodes lost its trade when Delos was made a free port, and a thousand leading Achaeans, among them the historian Polybius, were taken to Italy as hostages.
sum: The battle near Pydna in northern Greece in 168 BCE where a Roman army under the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus destroyed the army of Perseus, the last king of Macedon. It ended the Third Macedonian War.
